utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please go into private session before we call the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. Obviously, we expected to be an issue what should happen to the testimony of the last witness, Mr. Milan Babic. It is the Prosecution's position based on our review of the law and the facts in this case that the testimony should stand, it should be -- it should stay in the case and the Court should be permitted to rely on it and consider it. However, we recognise that this is going to be a disputed issue. What we propose is that we are willing to kind of initiate the procedure here, to get the ball rolling, to get this before the Court, in a proper way. So we are prepared to file a motion setting forth our position as to why we think the testimony can stay in the case and can be relied upon by the Chamber. We will be in a position to do that in approximately two weeks. We want to file as complete and thorough a motion canvassing the law on this issue as we can. And then obviously the Defence will have an opportunity to respond and then the Court can consider the issue and render its decision on it. That is our proposal. I've -- as I said, I've alerted the Defence to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting. It hadn't been anticipated by the Bench to deal with that issue at this point. However, the -- I will recognise you -- okay. Let me defer to you, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, bearing in mind what my colleague the Prosecutor has just said, the Defence wants to raise a very important matter. The Defence considers that we are not in a position to behave as if in the proceedings so far what happened did not happen. The tragically deceased Mr. Babic was a key Prosecution witness and with his 40 hours of testimony is what the entire indictment is based on. His examination was not completed. The examination-in-chief was conducted, the cross-examination reached halfway, and then with his tragic demise it was interrupted, which means quite literally that the witness wasn't examined fully, and his testimony is not complete because the Defence did not have a chance to cross-examine him in its entirety, nor did the Trial Chamber. So the testimony is invalid and therefore the Defence feels that it cannot be used in these proceedings. This fact alone, that is to say that his examination was not completed, leads to us making that conclusion, in the Defence's submission. In the meantime, we heard some facts that were made public via the information media, the mass media, and the spokesman for the Tribunal to the effect that Mr. Babic committed suicide. Now, if that fact is correct, and according to what the Defence knows at this point in time, that is indeed the case, then the question comes to mind of Mr. Babic's general capabilities and capacity of being a witness and testifying in this trial. So that's the second matter and second question which will need lead to an assessment of the validity of his testimony, that the Trial Chamber in the Defence's submission will have to make a ruling and take a stand. We also received a decision by the president of the Tribunal, according to which Judge Parker was appointed to investigate the circumstances which led to these tragic events. Once the investigation has been completed and when it has been established what took place, then possibly other important questions might be raised relevant to this trial but to other proceedings and other trials as well. At any rate the expense -- the Defence expects that Judge Parker's report will give us an answer to what actually happened to Mr. Babic during his testimony, whether there was any pressure excerpted upon him, whether there were any threats made against him, whether there were unlawful contacts with him, but before we receive a report of that kind, at this point in time I think that it would be beneficial if we were to stop presenting evidence and the Defence within a deadline of five or six days, will be sending in a written motion to the Trial Chamber presenting its views and position, and all the exhibits produced at this trial through that witness, together with his own testimony, in the Defence team's opinion, cannot be used. They should -- ought to be set aside from these proceedings and then the proceedings continue along their course as both sides see fit. Therefore, at this point in time the Defence considers that in the interests of justice and in the interests of the trial itself and the legality of the proceedings it would be opportune to interrupt the trial until we receive a copy of that report or until we come up with suggestions as to what should be done with the testimony. If what the Prosecutor has just put forward is accepted that would mean that one side has the right to hear a witness whereas the other side, through force of circumstance and objective conditions, has not been made possible because we were not able to complete our cross-examination, and the cross-examination was to have lasted another two days. This is a very serious matter and that is why I wish to raise it before this Trial Chamber and to ask that the matter be deferred. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. Actually when I spoke before you stood up I was trying to obviate just that. Let me see how we go on from here. Obviously, this is a very novel point which needs conversing legally and I do not think therefore that the Court or even the parties themselves are in a position to argue this point at this point in time. As a result, the Chamber is not in a position to determine whether or not the proceedings should be stopped now pending the report of Judge Parker. I do not think that the proceedings in Judge Parker's commission have a bearing on whether or not this case should proceed. Obviously, the parties, after researching the law and getting the facts will at some stage address the Chamber on the fate of Mr. Babic's evidence. That, in the Chamber's view, should not stop the Chamber from hearing further evidence from other witnesses in the interests of expedition. Therefore, the request by the Defence that the matter be adjourned until we've received a report from Judge Parker's commission is refused. The matter will proceed and the Court will take evidence from other parties -- from other witnesses. When the parties have prepared themselves on the question of Mr. Babic's evidence and at an appropriate moment, the parties will address the Court on what should be done with that evidence. Until then, that evidence just lies where it is until a determination is made. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are prepared to call our next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I believe we have to go -- it's Witness MM-003. I believe we have to go into private session to get the witness into the room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We have to do that, yes. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have heard your ruling. I have understood what you have just stated. May I just indicate a very important fact, however? When Mr. Babic was interviewed as a key Prosecution witness, many exhibits were presented, many facts were stated, of vital importance for the further -- for further proceedings and the Trial Chamber, the Defence and the Prosecution, I'm sure, in following the testimony, are under the direct influence or, rather, bear in mind the fact that it was Mr. Babic who was testifying. Now, what Mr. Babic testified about, or rather before a decision is made on the contents of his testimony, whether he could have been a witness, whether what he was talking about was valid, whether it is evidence in this trial, for that to be assessed and appraised in the proper way and for the proceedings and trial to go forward in the proper way, I think that the situation is such that the continuation of the trial with the existence of Mr. Babic's statement and testimony, without Trial Chamber ruling, goes to the detriment of the Defence and places it in an unequal situation. The Defence is not saying that any one is to blame for what happened. This is a tragic case. However, this tragic case gives rise to consequences and the consequences are such that we are going to hear more evidence while the Defence did not have a chance of completing its cross-examination of this key witness. In certain other systems, perhaps in the system from where -- Mr. Whiting's system, the one he comes from, there would automatically be perhaps an exclusion of the testimony and statement from the trial as being of no use but here we have a professional -- professional judges, and that's a privilege, that's a good thing. But if the rules state that the witness shall be examined through the examination-in-chief, through the cross-examination, which the Defence was doing, and which the -- and if the witness can be questioned by the Court, and then again by the Prosecution, et cetera, this did not happen. Then the survival of this incomplete testimony --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt you, Mr. Milovancevic? You are addressing the Chamber once again on an issue on which the Chamber has ruled and you are repeating the kind of things that you said before the Chamber ruled. I thought you were saying you just wanted to raise one important issue. You've now spoken for all of a whole page on the screen and I'm still trying to get the point. Either you get to the point or the Chamber will have to remind you that a ruling has been made on this point. What is your point, Mr. Milovancevic, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, briefly, Your Honour, because the new point is that the proposal was not linked to the investigation conducted by Judge Parker. That's a procedure set in place by the president of the Tribunal. I just indicated the fact that there was going to be an investigation under way which could provide the Trial Chamber with material which will make it better placed to decide and rule on the matter in the proper manner but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I interrupt you there? Hence, hence the Chamber's order that at an appropriate time, the parties will make submissions to the Chamber and the Chamber will then rule at that time and most probably part of the submission will include the report of the commission. I do not know. So what you have just said, I think, is more in line with what the Chamber has ruled on than in what you are suggesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we go into private session to bring the witness in, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber go into private session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, you could read the declaration now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may take your seat. You may take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, you may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Are you able to understand me in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I want to remind you that you've been granted protective measures by this Trial Chamber, which means that your name will not be used during the proceedings and your image will be distorted on the broadcasts of the proceedings. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You understand that also, if there are matters which could identify you, we'll move into private session to discuss those matters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, if at any time you don't understand me or you don't understand my question, please tell me.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You also have a glass of water next to you. Feel free to have some water and if you need more, it will be refilled for you. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, with the assistance of the usher I'm going to show you a sheet --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought maybe for the benefit of the witness and also for all of us participating in the Court, if you could tell him what his pseudonym is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I was just about to do that, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher I'm going to show you a piece of paper. The paper has the pseudonym number which is MM-003. Is your name also on that piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And could the usher please show that paper to the Defence. And could that paper now be shown to the Bench, please. And could that paper be made an exhibit under seal, please, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May that piece of paper that has just been shown around be made an exhibit and be given an exhibit number and may it then be placed under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 242, Your Honours, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So, witness, during these proceedings you'll be referred to either as "Witness" or by your number, "MM-003." Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in public session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, I want to draw your attention to the 17th of August 1990. Did something happen on that date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Around 3.00 in the afternoon, I was passing by the police station in Knin by car and I saw a lot of people gathered there. At that time, I was still unaware what was going on. Perhaps some time before that, rallies were often held so I wasn't really paying much attention as to what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you go to Golubic after you saw that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you saw when you went to Golubic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: After that I went to Golubic, and I saw at the youth settlement Golubic that there were quite a few people there. When I got there, I went in. On the left-hand side, in this little house, that was called the headquarters at the time of the youth drives formerly, there were some people there now who were giving out weapons to the people rallied there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who was there giving out weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Milan Martic, Miljenko Zelenbaba, Jovo Maric was at the top of the stairs, and Jovo Mitrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you know the identities of these people at the time or did you learn them later?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: At that time, I did not know the identity of Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: (redacted) so I knew him through football.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When did you learn the identity of Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Actually, later on, when night fell, my neighbour asked me to stay, or rather he didn't ask me to stay. He said I'd better stay there - I worked with them, for the radio station - so that the army would not mobilise me and send me off to the front line. That's where I found out that this was Milan Martic. Before that I had never seen him in my life. And, of course, the other participants too. They just said that it was Jovo Mitrovic. Well, actually I knew one of these men there. I didn't know that he was a member of the reserve and he told me that this was Jovo Mitrovic and that he was in charge of the reserve police in Knin. And then after that, another man went out of this little house. His name was Mirko Cenic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell us precisely what Milan Martic was doing on that day? What did you see him doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Nearby, a truck was parked, a small TAM truck, and boxes were unloaded from this truck and these boxes contained weapons. And then Jovo was writing this down, they all held some kind of pieces of paper where there were writing down the names of the people who they were giving weapons to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what was Mr. Martic doing exactly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: He was handing out weapons and when he would hand out a weapon he would tell Jovo the name, the name of that person was supposed to be written down by Jovo because they were making units already at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you learn which people were receiving weapons? Were they giving them to particular people or were they just giving the weapons to anybody?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Yes. Later on I found out that they were members of the reserve force who gathered in Golubic when they were given a certain signal that they all knew. They came from different directions, so they really came from all parts of the municipality of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you say "reserve force," reserve to what? Reserve force of what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: The reserve force of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, did you see Milan Babic on that day, on the 17th of August 1990?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was he there when you arrived or did he come later?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: He was already there by the time I arrived. He was -- he was there when I arrived. However, there was this big restaurant behind him, where these people who lived in this settlement got their meals, so quite a few after people after that left that restaurant. A lot of people, for example, leaders of the SDS from that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were you able to tell what Milan Babic was doing on that day, if anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: That day, I don't remember. I don't remember that he was doing anything. He was just present there and later on, that night, they talked for a long time, all these members of the SDS. At that time I actually didn't know that they were the Presidency of the SDS, and with Martic and with other people who were arriving. Actually, later on, I learned more and more about it because I was working there for the radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in public session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, you made reference earlier to barricades that started to be erected on the 17th of August 1990. Where were some of those barricades erected?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Well, the first barricades were erected by the village of Civljane and Polace, Padjeni, an area of Zrmanja, Rudele, Macure, Kosovo, Vrbnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What was the purpose of the barricades?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: At that time, as people were saying, it was in order to prevent the police force from Knin from coming in, the irregulars, and putting up the chequerboard flag in Knin and things like that, because already at that time, with the establishment of the Serb territories, the Serb territories were sort of established in that way in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said to prevent the police force from coming in. Which police force? A Serb police force or the Croatian police force?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: No. The Croatian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, were you afraid of the Croatian government?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: No. I never gave it much thought, about any difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you think that the Serbs in Croatia were threatened by the Croatian government at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: No. Certainly not at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You made a reference, Witness, to the chequerboard flag. Did the chequerboard flag make you afraid?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Well, I never actually -- I don't think I ever saw the chequerboard in my life. I didn't give it much thought. No, it had absolutely no influence on me, no effect. And it had no effect on most of the young people. Not only did they not feel any fear, they didn't give it any thought and didn't think about the differences between Serbs and Croats, for instance. So my answer is no, definitely no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The barricades or roadblocks that you made reference to, did they have any effect on the Croatian population?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Yes, they did. A great effect, great influence. Between the barricades at Polace and the barricades at Civljane, there was the village of Kijevo, the Croatian village of Kijevo, which was quite apart from any kind of communication lines, any communication from outside, and with any other part of Croatia. The only connection was to go across the hill and that would have taken, I don't know how many hours, to get to the next place.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I just want to be sure that I understand your answer because it gets translated to us. So are you -- do I understand you to be saying that Kijevo or the Croatian village of Kijevo was cut off by barricades?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Yes. That's it. That's the truth of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were there other villages like that, that you're aware of, that were cut off by barricades, other Croatian villages?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Well, for example, afterwards, when the barricade went up to Otisca then Vrlika, a small Croatian town, was left between the barricade at Civljane and Otisca.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, what was Milan Martic's role with respect to the barricades?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: As far as I understand it, from the first, he was the main commander for everything. He was the man who was organising, planning and managing the barricades.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness -- yes, Your Honour -- witness, after the break, I'll ask you how you knew that but now we've come to a point where it's convenient for a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. What do we do for the purpose of the witness? Do we go into private session so he exit or what happens?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think that what can happen is that the Court just adjourns for the break and the Court leaves, and then the TV goes off and then the witness is brought out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Court is adjourned, come back at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, we are still in public session. Before the break, you testified that Milan Martic was the main commander for everything, he was the man who was organising, planning and managing the barricades. How did you know that? Did you see it? Did you hear it? How did you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Well, already then, on that first day, in the evening, they said many things. The people who would come up there, they would talk about many things and you could see that all the things that were to be done and, as they said, new obstacles being erected, they talked to Martic. He tried to call up certain people and establish contact with people whom he already knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, do you know who was manning the barricades?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Well, the first barricades, it was mostly the reserve policemen who were given weapons from Martic in Golubic, on that day, and they were sent to those same places where they lived, in the villages where they lived, nearby where they lived. They were sent to these posts and they were the commanders of those barricades and those posts mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, at that time, or later, did Milan Martic talk about the barricades? Did he make statements about the barricades?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember that day that he spoke about that but later on, the following days, they discussed how to strengthen the barricades, because of breakthroughs, and in the meantime, the representatives of the JNA turned up, so that this was quite frequent after their departure. They talked to the politicians, to discuss what could be done next. When I say politicians, I mean members of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How long did the headquarters stay in Golubic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Well, about two weeks. The headquarters were in Golubic and afterwards we moved to another location from Golubic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where did you move to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: We went to Oton Polje, that location.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: During that two week period, how often was Milan Martic there in Golubic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: He slept there all the time. I don't remember exactly. He went home once or twice but he was there 24 hours, around the clock, because nothing could be decided without him at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: During the meetings that were held at Golubic, was -- were there any discussions or decisions made about what Milan Martic's role was going to be?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Well, at the very beginning, that was discussed too, as far as -- and as far as I was able to understand, Dr. Milan Babic was supposed to be the politician in charge of politics, whereas defence positions were to be led by Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you say defence positions, what do you mean exactly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: I mean the system of barricades that were erected around the Knin municipality, in the Serb places, and all the barricades -- or let me make things clear. When I say everything I mean all the barricades that were erected at the time and those that were going to be erected, to see how best this could be done, the best way to do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What was the relationship between Milan Martic and Milan Babic, that you were able to observe?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: At the beginning, it was fairly good and proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did that change?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: A little later, that relationship did start to change, mutual respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How did it change?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Well, already at that time, large quantities of material assistance began to come in, food, clothing, footwear, money, and the biggest problem was how to divide this up, distribute it. Babic wanted the bulk of it to go to the SDS or rather the party representatives, that they should discuss matters of that kind, whereas Martic wanted most of these goods, most of these resources to go to better equipped people, manage the barricades, for their food, for their clothing, footwear. So these material goods, their disputes were over these material goods and over money ultimately.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you hear at that time or later of something called the Council of National Resistance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Yes. That's when the Council for National Resistance was established, and there -- you had people from the SDS, with Martic and another member, Vitas. When I say member of the SDS, for example, there was Dusan Orlovic, there was Nebojsa Mandelic, there was David Rastovic for a time, and some others. I don't remember their names. And this included a reserve colonel Bogoljub Popovic. Then there was a Lieutenant Colonel who had retired. His name was not Stojanovic, Stojko Bjelanovic was his name. Perhaps I've left someone out but there were quite a few of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When did you first hear of the Council of National Resistance? When was it established to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: The Council for National Resistance was established in Golubic and at the very beginning, it was established as such, and I think there are written traces of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So when you say it was established in Golubic, is that at the time that the headquarters was in Golubic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I mean. The distribution of weapons, the headquarters was there, and that's when the Council of National Resistance was established. It was a body which was supposed to control the overall operations, both up at the barricades and later on. It was a sort of military coordination body.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, what was Milan Martic's role in the Council of National Resistance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: He was the commander of that council, and already before that he was appointed commander of the barricades of resistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How long did the Council of National Resistance last?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: As far as I remember, that council lasted until mid-November, I think, 1990, with the return of Martic to the station, because the radio station for communication was turned back to the centre for information in Knin and as far as I understand it -- stood it afterwards, that's where it came from in the first place, that's where it was taken from in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you say that Milan Martic returned to the station in mid-November of 1990, where was that station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: I apologise but I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You referred -- you said that Milan Martic returned to the station in mid-November of 1990. Can you just tell us what town or village that station is that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Well, after leaving and going to Oton, the station was transferred to a different location for a few days, but it ended up at Sinobadova Glavica and it was transferred to the information centre in Knin after that. The location was called Sinobadova Dom.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when did it return to Knin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: With Martic's return to the police station. I can't give you the exact day but it was November.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Was Milan Babic a part of the Council of National Resistance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: I can't say now. I don't really know what his role was exactly at that time but I know that he was present at all the meetings and most of the decisions. He generally listened and attended all those meetings that they had and where they took decisions. I can't say exactly what his function was. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we go into private session, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, you told us earlier that in -- sometime in November, Milan Martic returned to the station in Knin. Did there come a time when the police in the Krajina became organised?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: As far as I understood things, when he returned to the station, sometime mid-November, say the 15th of November, quite simply there was the necessary stability for his return to the station. The police had accepted him as the chief of police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And then after he returned, did there come a time when the police in the Krajina became organised?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Yes. It became stronger and more organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were people appointed to positions at police stations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Actually, at the time when he returned to the station, many things had changed there. I remember that Gojko Drvenje [phoen], the then commander, was still creating problems. In terms of popularity he had prevailed so everything was kind of over and he could choose who he'd work with at the station, but as far as I managed to find out, these signatories of this petition, people knew in advance that Zelenbaba, Cenic, and Orlovic would be his associates.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And where did they work, those people that you've just told us, Zelenbaba, Cenic, and Orlovic? Were they in Knin or some other place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: No, they were in Knin. Cenic and Zelenbaba were policemen. I think Zelenbaba was an inspector and Cenic was a policeman and Dusan Orlovic was a man who had studied medicine. He said himself that he had studied it for about 15 years and never graduated. So they were at the Knin police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did Dusan Orlovic to your knowledge get a position at some point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Yes. Later on, he became head of the state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately when that happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: I think that that was later, sometime in January 1991, because at that time, new police chiefs had been appointed in the broader area of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who appointed these new police chiefs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: The new police chiefs were appointed by Martic, all of them. Well, more or less he knew a lot of these people because he studied in Zagreb so he knew them from his studies in Zagreb and from the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell us by, say, January of 1991 or around there, can you tell us which police chiefs have been appointed in which villages?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: As for SUP Knin, Miljenko Zelenbaba was appointed and Nikola Manovic. For a long time they were his closest co-workers. As for Benkovac, Bosko Drazic had already been appointed. For Obrovac, Zeljko Jelic. For Gracac, Marko Dragicevic. For Korenica, Bosko Rapajic. In Srb, Nikola Vojvodic. In Lapac, Dujo Vojvodic. I know that he and Nikola were brothers. As for Civljani, Dragan Knezevic was appointed at the time but in Civljani, the only difference was that there had never been a police station there before. It was sort of like a forward post of Knin because it was between the Croat village of Kijevo and a Serb village Borika.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What about Okucani? Was somebody appointed there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: For Okucani, Krsta Zarkovic. Later on, he became head of the special police forces. It was called the PJM, the special police units.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How about in Vojnic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: In Vojnic, it was Toso Pajic, because he had the greatest authority there. I don't know what Milos Pajic was to him then but at that time he was head of state security in Dvor Na Uni, Nikola Bolajic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now you said that Milos Pajic was head of state security but you told us earlier that Dusan Orlovic became head of state security.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Milos Pajic was head of state security for Kordun Banija. Dusan Orlovic was head of state security for Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, were you able to observe what Milan Martic's relationship was to all of these police chiefs that you've just identified?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: These relationships were excellent. They were better than good.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What kind of control, if any, did Milan Martic have over the police in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: He had 100 per cent control over the police because he was by far the most popular person within the police, and he had a great deal of credit, a great deal of merit, because of the signing of the petition which was in 1990. All of that was something that was held to his credit and he was considered to be a great Serb. Later on, even more so when he established relations with people in Belgrade. Then he had 100 per cent support. He was the man in charge, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'll ask you some more questions about people -- relations with Belgrade in a moment. In -- by, say, January of 1991, would Milan Martic have meetings with these various chiefs in these villages that you've identified? Would he meet with them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Well, he tried to have these operative meetings, as they were called. They were supposed to be held on Mondays and if they couldn't come, depending on where they were, depending on the positions where they were, and the development of the situation, then somebody would come on their behalf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What was discussed at these meetings, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: I did not attend the meetings but I know, because in a way I was with him practically non-stop so he talked about many things through these people, he actually tried to strengthen the establishment of the Serb territory, that things would be as stable as possible so that people would be safe, so that the Ustashas - he called them the Ustashas - could not penetrate into Serb territories, and the achievement of some plans that he knew about, in advance, or that somebody else had planned previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, at this time, now we are in January or so of 1991, did you think that there was a danger from the Ustashas, as they were being called at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: No, no. I never gave it any thought. No, I didn't feel anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, did you learn if Milan Martic gave any orders to the police chiefs in these operative meetings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Yes. That was the point of these meetings, that they should be given instructions as to what they should do next and how to help areas where, in a way, there was no Krajina Police. At that time, they were called the Martic police. So for these Serb settlements, they tried to find a way out, those that didn't have barricades or a Serb police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, at that time, did Milan Martic talk about the barricades and whether they had accomplished anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: At that time, the way in which he was satisfied was that finally Serb territories were established in part, but he didn't have enough weapons, and there wasn't a general feeling in favour of going to these other areas so that they should be taken and made into a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I am just not sure I understood the end of your answer. You said there wasn't a feeling in favour of going into these other areas. Can you explain that a little more? It may have been a translation problem or maybe I just didn't understand your answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Well, a way was sought as to how the territories that were outside the barricades -- I mean a way was sought through the police stations that were the closest to those places that did not belong to the SAO Krajina yet, or rather had not become part of the Serb Krajina, the Serb territories yet. I don't know how to say this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand. What was Milan Martic's view on trying to find ways to reach out, to expand to these areas that were not yet part of the SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: He got a signal from Belgrade that he would get whatever is necessary, money, financial resources, in order to establish or rather to go to those places to establish as many police stations as he could in all these Serb places according to a map that had been previously made because there were already some negotiations between the army, him and the Croatian side, to open unhindered communications, to remove the barricades, or to have some other kind of blockade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you said earlier that JNA officials came even to the headquarters in Golubic back in August or September of 1990. At this time, in January of 1991, did Martic have meetings with JNA officials?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honours. The witness spoke about retired or other JNA officers. He never mentioned, as far as I could remember, JNA officials in his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Just a moment, Your Honour, please. Your Honour, on page 34, line 23, the witness said, "I don't remember that day that he spoke about that," and that was a reference to August 17th, "but later on the following days they discussed how to strengthen the barricades because of breakthroughs and in the meantime, the representatives of the JNA turned up." That was what I was relying on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You see that, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see a difference between officials and representatives. Let the witness explain what he meant by that. Perhaps that would be the best way to resolve the matter, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you like to do that, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I'll just go to the question, which was in -- around, by January of 1991, did Milan Martic meet with representatives or officers or officials of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Yes. He did, and even before that. Well, directly, he talked a lot with Tolimir and Pecanac. I knew Pecanac for years before that, but I didn't know about Tolimir. He was a counterintelligence officer and then in January 1991, the then commission or the federal Secretariat, as far as I can remember now, that is to say from each and every republic there was one secretary and a representative of the military for the military district -- military naval district from Split. From there came a high ranking naval officer Ljubomir Bera [phoen]. I was there myself when they came. I was in Martic's offers. And when they walked in and sat down, I went out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, witness, at this time, at the end of 1990, beginning of 1991, do you know how the police in the Krajina were paid?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Payments were made without any lists or anything. It was cash for the most part. Somewhere -- at first it would be in kind, clothing, footwear, food, depending on what was available. That was one of the main reasons for the quarrels between Dr. Babic and Martic. Later, however, another thing happened too. Martic got certain quantities of money from Belgrade. The first one I know was Frenki. I just know that name, Frenki.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: That happened sometime after Martic returned to the station, so it should be mid-November, beginning of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, I'll ask you some questions about that in just a moment. You said that the police were paid in cash. Did Milan Martic have any role in the payment of -- the payment to police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: It wasn't that he was directly handing out the money to the policemen. This was done by the women who worked at the accounting department, and through chief Zelenbaba, whereas he personally would take out the money that he had in his safe and then he would count the money and give out as much as they were supposed to give out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who would take the money out of his safe? Who were you referring to there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Martic. He was the only one who had the key and the code that was in his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who would he give the cash to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Well, to the commanders of stations, depending on who would come, the commander or the chief or whoever represented that police station. I know Zelenbaba, for instance, I was there several times when he gave him money.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you made reference in your answer to two blue PUCH vehicles. Where were these vehicles coming from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: These were vehicles of the MUP of Serbia, according to their licence plates.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you said that there were some policemen who were running from the station. Why were they running from the station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Because they didn't know who the vehicles belonged to. They thought that it was the Croatian police, and that's why they were running away from the station.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who was in these vehicles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: In the first vehicle was Frenki, and inspector Kostic was in the other one. I think his first name was Rade. Judging by the way he spoke I think he came somewhere from Baranja.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This person, Frenki, do you know what his position was? Where did he work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: That first time I didn't know at all. I didn't know who Frenki was or where he came from or actually it wasn't clear to me at all what these people were looking for over there, what was going on at that moment, when I saw them. But later on, I realised what it was all about. Martic told me a lot about this, or actually this was one of the kinds of support that came in. For example, they openly started saying at that time that they went to Bosansko Grahova, that these people did not come directly to Knin. They would leave their load with their man in Bosanska Grahovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. We have to take this one step at a time. I'll ask you some questions about that, about Bosanska Grahovo, in a moment. But later, did you learn -- you said you learned some things later. Did you learn what Frenki's position was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what did you learn it to be?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: My understanding was that he was assistant chief of state security of Serbia, assistant to Jovica Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Now, on this occasion when he came to Knin with the two vehicles, did they bring anything in those vehicles, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: In the vehicles, well, I don't know exactly what the number was. I personally unloaded the two vehicles at the police garage, and there were automatic and semi-automatic rifles there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did Frenki meet with Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Yes. He went to his office. I went with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did Milan Martic tell you anything about -- afterwards, about that meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Yes. He said to me that he had received money from Belgrade. This money was supposed to be used for salaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were there other occasions, to your knowledge, that Frenki brought money to Knin from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: After that, he came more and more often, and he brought this money, this cash, and some other stuff, in a bag.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: For the most part, I would see it. I can't say that I saw the money directly but it was the same bags that were being brought, and after that, Martic would usually make comments because he'd be in a good mood. Obviously he would receive what he had asked for.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you made a reference to Bosanska Grahovo. Can you explain that a little more? What did you learn about what was happening there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: As time went on, Martic and Dusan Orlovic would talk more and more about things that were happening. They would happen in advance. They would talk in advance, how it came to erecting the barricade or rather the weapons coming from Belgrade were at the bottom of the truck, for instance, and on top of the weapons would be construction material or bricks. And since in the MUP of Serbia, as far as I understood it, Pakrac was the assistant head for state security for Kosovo and Metohija, and originally, he was from Crni Lug a village near Bosanska Grahovo, where they had the bases for the first unloading of weapons. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: (redacted) the brother of Uros Pakrasac was Jovica, and Jovica lived in Bosanska Grahovo permanently.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could just have a redaction at lines 18 and 19 there? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have a redaction. What do you want specifically to be redacted there?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Just those two lines, 18 and 19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Could we redact lines 18 and 19 at page 51, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, witness, did you learn when weapons started to come in trucks to Bosanska Grahovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: As I understood it, it began sometime in September 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did you learn what happened to the weapons once they arrived there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: All these goings to Bosanska Grahovo, it was just Martic and Dusan Orlovic who knew about that and they would transfer this with a small car, a Lada Niva car. They would transport it to Knin and then later on, to certain parts of the territory, if they thought that part needed more weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, later, later on, in January and February of 1991, did weapons come to the Krajina or to Knin in any other way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: I think that sometime at the end of January, it began coming in, in trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where were these trucks coming from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: The trucks belonged to the MUP of Serbia and they were coming in from Serbia, because sometime in January, 1991, one of those trucks went off the road. There were two trucks, Mercedes trucks, light blue, the colour was, and the last, the second truck turned over, went off the road and turned over and all the weapons poured out of it and lay around about. And the Bosanska Grahovo police came in, the Sarajevo command was still respected and the commander was a man by the name of Tica and there were a lot of problems with the Knin police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we go into private session, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, who was present when that truck overturned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: When we arrived up there, there was Frenki there, and his man from security, a man that drove the truck. He was very angry because he had done that. Let me just mention that part was called Kesici, the village of Kesici, just before Bosanska Grahovo. Frenki, that is to say, Frenki was extremely angry because this other man had done that and because of the problems that he had with the Grahovo police, and Martic contacted Pokrajac who was already in Grahovo and he was supposed to find another truck to replace the other one, to load up and to deal with the Grahovo chief of police, to prevent him making any problems for what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did that happen? Did another truck come and load up the weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The second truck arrived, they loaded up the weapons, and it left.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, how do you know that the two Mercedes trucks were from the MUP of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Well, the people -- first of all there was Frenki. Then the escort, the escorts were wearing special police uniforms from Serbia, and thirdly there were the licence plates that you could put up and take down very quickly, and after that, some white licence plates were put on. But that time, those two trucks were left in Knin so that they could use them, and then they were the blue police licence plates, the blue ones of the MUP of Serbia. I knew that the first number was M 602. That was the first number on the licence plates, the MUP of Serbia, belonging to the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, witness, you spoke earlier about Frenki coming to Knin in around November of 1990. And you talked about -- you learned that he brought money. Did he and the people he was with do anything else on that trip in Knin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: The second time he appeared, with Uros Pokrajac, was sometime towards the end of November and beginning of December 1991, when they arrived, he was called to a meeting by the then president of the SDS, Dr. Babic, and in fact it was a special team that was supposed to do away with and clear up the telephone lines from the bugs, interception on the part of the Croatian side, so that the line was a clean line and couldn't be listened into by the Croatian side. So that's what they did. There was a technical team of specialists. And there was a man in that group who was a specialist for picking locks, for example, so picking locks, looking at the posts coming in, and while they were cleaning up in Dr. Babic's office, they found bugs, listening devices, bugs placed in the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, who did Milan Martic meet with in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: First of all, Frenki, Radmilo Bogdanovic, and Jovica Stanisic. Radmilo Bogdanovic was the Minister of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what was Jovica Stanisic's position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: He was the chief of the RDV, the state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What was the purpose of the trip, as you learned it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: As far as I heard, the purpose was to receive equipment, money, and support, quite simply support, for expanding the barricades to take in as many police stations as possible, to extend Serb territories by that token.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What did Milan Martic tell you about the meetings after the trip? What did he tell you had happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: He said that he was quite satisfied with talks and that he was given promises that everything he needed he would get, that he should just continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: After this trip, do you know if Milan Martic had other meetings with Jovica Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where did these meetings occur?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: After that, he would go to Belgrade often, to meetings with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know if Jovica Stanisic ever came to Knin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: I know for the first time that he was in Martic's flat in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you learn about a car accident that Jovica Stanisic had been involved in at some point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: I learned about that before we went to Belgrade, because often when we would travel to Lika, and pass a place called Malovan, Orlovic

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Malovan, he would say, "This is where Jovica Stanisic had an accident in September or October of 1990," and when you go around the bend there or down the slope they would show the house where they got assistance to pull out the Mercedes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will just need a redaction there at lines 17 and 18, please, of page 58.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May we have line 17 and 18 at page 58 redacted, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Witness, after January of 1991, that first meeting that you were aware of, between Martic and Stanisic, do you know if they also communicated by telephone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: When -- well, sometime in 1990, November, or December, when they were cleaning up the municipality of the bugging devices and the Knin station, he was given a telephone, a direct telephone link, to Stanisic, a direct telephone line, and they established that telephone line by -- or, rather, technicians from Serbia set up that line.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Witness, could you tell the Judges, please, how did Milan Martic talk about Jovica Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: He was with him -- or rather he was very enthusiastic about him. He liked him 100 per cent, kept referring to him as my brother. He came to like him very much, because anything he asked for, he would always get. So he thought of him as his own brother, and he would refer to him very often as "my brother Jovica." He never questioned that Jovica would do anything he asked him for and before that, he would mention the name Ledeni, meaning frozen. I didn't know what this nickname Ledeni meant but he, Uros Pokrajac, explained it to me afterwards, because he would bring up the name Ledeni very often and Ledeni was used to refer to Jovica Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know if Milan Martic had any meetings with Slobodan Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How did you learn that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Stanisic's office, and somebody would take us to take him over from Milosevic's office, from where Milosevic's office was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll need another redaction from line -- page 60, line 3 to line 8, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. May lines 3 to 8 of page 60 please be redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Whiting, before we proceed, I'd like to suggest that you issue the caution to the witness which you had given previously concerning the nature of - you know what I'm referring to, that certain thing - and so that we avoid you having to ask for a redaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think that's a good idea. For that purpose could we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I just have one or two more questions on this topic and then if we could -- thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, when you heard the -- Milan Martic talk about Milosevic, how did he talk about Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: He used different nicknames, sometimes he would refer to him as Slobo when everything was going okay. When I say -- well, if everything were to go well, and he would get everything he wanted, he would be satisfied.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did he use any other nicknames for him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: He would say, "The boss."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. I think -- so he used -- he would refer to him as the boss?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: As far as I know, and I heard this fairly often, he would say, "the boss," "Gazda." Slobo -- well, the name was Slobodan so if you said Slobo that was a friendly term, whereas if you said, Gazda, the boss, that was more a mark of respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think this would be a convenient time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Court is adjourned and we will come back at quarter to six.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, when the camp at Golubic began functioning in March or April of 1991, who was being trained there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Special Forces of the police of Krajina were being trained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who did the training?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: The training was conducted by Captain Dragan with his assistants, Mark, one was Mark. I know his name was Mark. He introduced him as an Irishman. The other one was Fico. Actually, this Fico said after a while that he came from the state security of Serbia, that he was Frenki's man.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you describe the training? What kind of training was done?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Walls were constructed there, and it sort of looked like training grounds or for keeping the police or military fit and trained, so it was typical of this kind of military training grounds or police training grounds and also for using weapons. And he trained them in order to be able to work in groups that would then be brought together.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How long would the training last? That is, for a particular person, officer, who went there, how long would the training last?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: The training was supposed to last for up to two months. Now, the length of the training at that moment depended on the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What kind of equipment was at the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: The trainees, the people who actually went there to train, they had infantry weapons, and also on the side, there were six cannons all the time, some kind of old cannons, I don't know the type, and in the meantime a tank was brought in, self-propelled. I think it was 76 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What kind of vehicles were there at the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: At first, as soon as it was established, six new Landrovers were brought in, white ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who brought those in, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: It came from the MUP of Serbia, with Frenki.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did those Landrovers have any special characteristics or special abilities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Well, these were field vehicles that could take up to nine to ten men. They had very good performance capacities. 101, 104, 106, were their numbers. I think some of them were also given to the police station in Knin later for the intervention Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What kind of communications equipment was available at Golubic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: In Golubic, at that time, both for training and for equipping the special units, special equipment was used, special equipment provided by Frenki, walkie-talkies, special radio transmitters that could be heard even further away without support from a repeater.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was there a shooting range at Golubic or nearby?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Well, yes. To the north, four or five kilometres to the north. Gnjile Bare was the location's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what other villages to the north, if you keep going, what village do you arrive at?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: You'd arrive at the village of Strmica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What kind of weapons were at the shooting range?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: For the most part, weapons that people who were involved in the training would get. They would be reassigned to other places afterwards or units, so weapons for shooting, and they even tried out the self-propelled tank, 76 millimetres. Later on, they tried out yet another weapon, that they had just worked on. It was called the armoured train.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who constructed the armoured train?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: The armoured train was made at Frenki's request.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How was the camp paid for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I really did not understand this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What I meant was, all these things that you're talking about, all this equipment and all these things at the camp, who paid for them? Where did the money come from for the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Most of the equipment or all of the equipment was brought from Frenki's -- from Belgrade by Frenki, the equipment and the money. He's the one who decided with his appointed commanders about everything. He's the one who had the money, who paid these people, and who brought in the equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What was Milan Martic's role at the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: The camp was under the command of Milan Martic. At that time Frenki -- or rather he and Frenki were on good terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember any of the people who -- any of the men who trained there at the beginning, at the camp, by name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: I remember that Dragan Karana went, Milovic Janovic [phoen], Milan Lukic, Goran Opacic and his two brothers, I don't know, I can't remember their names. They were called the Opacic brothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where were the Opacic brothers come from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: They came from Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did the men who were being trained have to do something at the end of their training?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: They were supposed to carry out their direct tasks, in order to show what they had learned, especially movement, establishment movement in formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did something happen at Ljubovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Ljubovo was carried out by a generation from Golubic. As far as I understood, that was a former Croatian farm by the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What do you understand happened at Ljubovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: My understanding was that they fully carried out their task because they managed to use hand held rocket launchers and to fire at these facilities where they had been sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. We have to just get a little bit of explanation here. Who was sent there and who carried out this attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: At that time, the people who had carried out this training or rather the people who had been trained were called Martic's men, Marticevci. That's the name they got. And I know that the platoon commander was Lieutenant Calic, Milorad Calic. They were people who had completed this training in Golubici that had been carried out by Captain Dragan.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And they did the attack on Ljubovo, this group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Yes. They carried out their assignment. They successfully attacked Ljubovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And was Ljubovo a Croatian village or a Serb village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Ljubovo was a purely Croatian village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you said that they used hand held rocket launchers, they fired those at the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Yes. Because after the action, they celebrated, they were pleased with what they had done. They said that openly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And do you know what the result was of the attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: As far as I understood things, there were a few persons who got killed and injured. This man who was from the area told me that this had been carried out very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, the men who were trained at Golubic, what happened -- what did they do after their training? Where did they go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: They went back to where they had been sent from for this training. They had this first assignment that they carried out and then they went back to their formation units or rather the places from where they had been sent originally.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what would they do there? What would be their function there when they returned to where they had been sent from originally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: They had the status of special police. They were better-paid, they had vehicles at their disposal, quite simply they had many more benefits and enjoyed a higher reputation because they were sort of the strike force in a way. They were invincible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And after they returned to where they were -- had come from, what was their relationship to Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: They were under his command. They had maximum respect for him. And they carried out whatever he asked for.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Witness, at Easter time in 1991, did something happen in Plitvice?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Yes. There was a clash there between Martic's police that was supposed to take Plitvice and the Croat forces, the police forces in the MUP, that were there. They clashed. These were two forces that clashed actually. On the Serb side, one man got killed, two were wounded, and two were arrested by the Croatian MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know who was in command of the Serb side, of the Serb unit at Plitvice?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: The commander of the Serb side was Djurica Manovic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did somebody send him there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Martic selected him to be the leader of that special company that was sent out to take Plitvice.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: This was done from Golubic. This was absolutely not hidden.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you told us earlier in your testimony that in January of 1991, Milan Martic was in command of the police. Did he remain in command of the police throughout 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did there come a time when Milan Babic tried to get control?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember approximately when that was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly but there were two attempts. One was -- well, I know the name was Lazikovic Slavko [phoen], he was a Professor. And the second attempt involved the appointment of Dusan Vjestica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was Milan Babic successful? Was he able to get control of the police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
