utterances.text: No. He didn't stand a chance.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Why do you say he didn't stand a chance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Because Martic had a great deal of authority, and he didn't have any chance of upsetting that, and already at that time he had support from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What about the TO? In the summer and the fall of 1991, who commanded the TO in the SAO Krajina, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: The TO had a joint staff with Martic, established sometime I think in July 1991 at the fortress of Knin. That's where they joint staff was. He was -- or rather without his command, nothing could be done. He was issuing orders to the commander of the Territorial Defence as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: To your mind, was there any difference between TO officers or soldiers and the police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Technically speaking, apart from the equipment and training, there was no difference. The command was the same. It's just that the older members of the Territorial Defence had a different uniform but all the rest was the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You talked earlier about the conflict between Milan Babic and Milan Martic. Did that continue during 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did one of them receive more support from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Martic got more and more support and assistance from Belgrade. On the other hand, Babic was losing a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did there come a time when Milan Martic had a dispute with Frenki?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: That was sometime in June or July, because Martic established the staff at the fortress and transferred it from Golubic to the fortress, together with the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know what the dispute was about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: As Martic said, Frenki would allow himself to do a great many things and he was increasingly taking control over people, and he didn't like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did Frenki leave Knin or the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: For how long?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly for how long, but at any rate, the other part of the territory in Korenica was involved. Let me explain this. When there was this quarrel, when the Golubic camp was closed down, then Captain Dragan's people, together with Bosko Bozovic [phoen], and agreement with Bosko Bozovic, the president of the SDS from Korenica. So part of Captain Dragan's people were transferred to Korenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what did Frenki do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: First he returned to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did he stay in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Not for a long time. When the new camp was established, in the territory of Korenica, that motel, that location was called Sesta licka.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when that happened, did he return to Korenica? Frenki, that is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: It's not that he returned the way he had been in Golubic. In Golubic he would spend -- he would spend a lot of his time there actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So do I understand you correctly that he would go -- he went back to Korenica -- he went to Korenica but he didn't spend as much time there as he had spent in Golubic? Is that -- am I understanding you correctly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, when Martic transferred in June or July to the fortress in Knin, did he remain based there after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Yes. They stayed there for quite a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I want to ask you some questions about Lovinac. Did there come a time when something happened there in Lovinac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was in June, Lovinac was a Croat village between Gracac, Licki Gracac, and Medak. It was quite a hindrance, in terms of communicating with the Serb area, Medak/Citluk so it was attacked early in the morning by Martic's police, from two different directions. On one side there was the armoured train from the direction of Gracac, and from Medak, there was mortar fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What was Martic's role in the attack, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: He was in command. He was at Udbina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What -- what was the result of the attack on the village? What happened to the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Well, you could see smoke and what was going on. Later on, he asked for a Croatian radio to be found in order to hear what the effects were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And do you know what the effects were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: According to the stories, there were casualties and wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know what the effect was on the Croat population in that village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: They were in a panic. They wanted to leave, to escape, and that was the object of the attack, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness is talking about what could be heard over the radio, and the question was, what was the effect on the Croatian population. How can the witness know that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was just about to ask how he knew that but I was going to ask that we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Still trying to understand. Mr. Milovancevic says the witness is talking about what could be heard over the radio. I'm trying to look at when "radio" was first spoken about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have it at line 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Yeah, line 11 says "later on he asked for a Croatian radio to be found in order to hear what the effects were." I don't know who is this who asked for a Croatian radio to ask, to find out the effects. I'm not quite sure how that statement relates to the question that is being asked, if this witness knows the effect of that attack on the village. And this is what I'm trying to understand, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. It's out of context. We don't know the context from which the witness is stating what he's stating. The witness wasn't on the spot. He doesn't know any thing directly, has no direct knowledge. He is speaking in an indirect way. And then he's telling it in the way that makes it completely difficult to understand what was going on, and then he didn't say that he had any direct information, personal information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, did the witness say he was not on the spot at any stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm just starting out from what the witness has been telling us so far in response to questions asked him by the Prosecution. I'm not saying what the witness is stating but I can see that the witness is talking about something that he doesn't know firsthand or he cannot know firsthand, at least judging on the answers he gave. He says that somebody asked for the Croatian radio to be switched on so that they could hear what the effects were on the village and then the next question by the Prosecution was how did the Croatian population behave? There must be a link or grounds laid for that kind of question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't know whether you answered my question. My question was simply was the witness -- has the witness ever said he was not on the spot. You haven't answered that. That's okay. Mr. Whiting, maybe if you could just clarify these points and let's find out, if you can separate the knowledge of the witness from the radio and deal with the radio separately, it would be a great help.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour, and it had been my intention to do that but in -- if we could move in private session to get the basis of his knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We will do that. Will that clear the point, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, from what you were able to hear, were you able to know what the relationship was between the police and the JNA at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: As I saw it, and as far as I know, it was excellent, more than excellent. In fact, they were on a joint assignment, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know what that joint assignment was, from what you were able to observe and hear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Well, it was a joint cooperation and a joint task, joint assignment, for joining up all the Serb lands into one entity, one whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you hear any discussion about what would happen to Croat villages that were in that area, that were in the way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Those -- well, those villages were to be cleansed, quite simply, because they were in the way, towards opening communications, towards Serb territory, and as I understood it, along certain axes, directions, the direction to Lika, for example, the entire line was to be moved towards Gospic, up to Gospic, so you had pure villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you say those villages were to be cleansed, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: That meant that the Croatian population should either leave under these actions or to -- or simply that they should be there no longer, to leave the territory, to leave those villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you ever have any conversations with Milan Martic about Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Well, I remember when we passed by that way, or close by, towards Vojnic on the road towards Vojnic, he would frequently tell me about the parliament, the Sabor.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Or rather, sorry, the Sabor was a Croatian village, interpreter's correction. Saborsko. In the Plaski municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And when he contacted Medo, and Medo, as far as I understood it was the president or whatever of the SDS, and that that village was in the way, and on one occasion, well, we would go quite frequently. On different occasions, he would say -- he would talk about, "Well, we fucked their mothers. Now this is pure Serb land," and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you learn anything about who had carried out the operation in Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: As for the operation in Saborsko, he said that the forces that had already become the Red Berets took part in that when they were transferred from Golubic. They changed their name. They were no longer the Marticevci, Martic's men. Now they had become the Red Berets. Because actually for a very short period of time, they were Marticevci at Golubic and at the Knin fortress they were called Knindzas because of this little bear that was a symbol of these fighters. So together with the army they moved against that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The -- these forces that you say had become the Red Berets at that time, do you know if they were under Martic's command at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Yes. They were under Martic's command.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How about Skabrnja? Did you have any conversation with Milan Martic about what had happened at Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: As for Skabrnja, he talked about Goran Opacic considerably. They kept thinking that this man was fool, a fool, that he was crazy. So Skabrnja was sort of a symbol. He kept saying, "Goran Opacic or the Opacic brothers, they had really done their job, they had really fucked them, they completed this mission."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did he talk about what the mission was in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Yes. This mission meant to liberate the entire area towards Zemunik, towards Zadar, I don't know the exact name of the area and to cleanse it from the Croat population.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was Goran Opacic under Martic's command at the time this operation was carried out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Yes. He was a member of the Benkovac special police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: During this time period, did -- August through December of 1991, did Milan Martic go to places where fighting had occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Well, yes. He often went out to visit, because people's morale would be boosted when he would be nearby, when he would visit them. That was very important, when he showed up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were there problems that you were aware of that occurred where fighting had occurred, problems with the police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: These problems for the most part were of a material nature, as I like to put it. It was major theft. The army accused the police of taking everything away from the places that they would enter, cleansing them of everything that could be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what did Martic do about this, to your knowledge? How would he deal with these problems, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: He didn't like that. He wanted to prevent that, but he simply didn't know how to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: He wanted to prevent what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: He wanted to prevent this rivalry between the army and the police. He didn't believe that the police was doing that, that they were taking these things away.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know if he did anything to stop that theft from occurring? Or do he just not believe that it was occurring?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Well, he changed the commanders of the police in those villages where there were major problems and where he had indications of things like that going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you about Kijevo. Did something happen in Kijevo at the beginning of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Yes. At the beginning, beginning of 1991, Vaso Pecer was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And who was Vaso Pecer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: Vaso Pecer was a young man who was at the barricades. He was from the village of Polace right next to the Croat village of Kijevo. In a way, they were neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was he a Serb or a Croat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: A Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did anything happen after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: His body remained facing a hill called Bat [phoen]. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003
utterances.text: (redacted) When we got there, Babic was supposed to calm these people down, these people were already there assembled. They were upset. The family of the killed man was there, and then this colonel came, I don't remember what his rank was, but Lieutenant Colonel Djukic, Borislav, who was the commander of the army in that area, he said, "You cannot pass that way." And then Tolimir showed up and then they explained that it was dangerous for him to go up there. If he went up there he might get killed. And then we went back. Now, I don't know, a day or two later, thanks to Tolimir, they got the body out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we'll need a redaction just at the beginning of that answer, the first few lines at the beginning of that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, I have some questions for you about Kijevo, about something that happened later at Kijevo but we've reached the end of the session for today so I'll have to ask you those questions tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which lines specifically did you want redacted?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Lines -- on page 89, lines 12 and 13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May lines 12 and 13 of page 89 please be redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And line 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: There is a suggestion that line 10 also be redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The problem here is that we are looking at two different monitors. It's line 12 -- it's line 12 and 13 on the Court monitor and on the English -- on the LiveNote monitor, it's line 9 and 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You want 9 and 10. Do you want to redact "his body remained facing the hill called ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, it's "from that afternoon ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: "From that afternoon ..." Could that be redacted, please, that would be line 9 and 10 on the LiveNote monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think it's a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The matter stands down -- stands adjourned to tomorrow. We'll come back here tomorrow at quarter past two in the afternoon, in the same court.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I thought it was in the morning. I think we've been moved to the morning session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. If we have been --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: At nine in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We will start at nine in the morning, instead of quarter past two in the afternoon. Thank you so much. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
